metadata.title: Importance of students’ social resources for their academic achievement and well-being in elementary school

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the German PIRLS 2016 sample of Grade 4 students and applies regression models with heteroskedasticity-robust, school-clustered standard errors to account for the nested structure of PIRLS data (students within schools). The manuscript does not report the use of complex sampling weights (e.g., student/sampling weights such as W_FSTUWT) or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Instead, the authors focus on robust inference and on variable selection and imputation procedures (stacked adaptive LASSO with multiple imputation). Because the paper does not document weight variables, the analysis should be interpreted as primarily relying on model-based estimation with cluster-robust SEs rather than population-representative weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the German PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 representative sample (N=3959). Outcomes and predictors were drawn from PIRLS student, parent, teacher, and principal questionnaires plus administrative information for academic track recommendation. The analytic sample sizes vary by variable in Table 1 (e.g., academic track recommendation N=3856; enjoyment of school N=3493; bullying N=3454; teacher support N=3333), indicating that analyses rely on multiple imputation (50 imputations) to address missingness rather than complete-case restriction. No additional grade or school-type restrictions are described beyond the Grade 4 PIRLS target population.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Germany Grade 4 (Reading context; academic track recommendation proxy)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 1 (SRF only): R2=0.081; bullying coefficient β=-0.062 (SE=0.009, p<0.001); teacher support β=0.100 (SE=0.011, p<0.001). Model 3 (SRF + post-double selection controls): R2=0.351; bullying β=-0.011 (SE=0.009, not significant); teacher support β=0.025 (SE=0.009, p<0.001). Sensitivity (many-worlds): Model 4 R2=0.631 (bullying β=0.002; teacher support β=0.002, both not significant); Model 6 R2=0.448 (bullying β=0.005; teacher support β=0.002, not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Germany Grade 4 the study leveraged experienced bullying and perceived teacher support to predict academic track recommendation, finding that bullying’s negative association attenuated to near zero after post-double selection controls and became statistically non-significant in the richer “many-worlds” specifications, while teacher support effects also shrank substantially. This indicates that social interaction factors may not provide robust incremental explanatory power for academic track placement once a broad set of student, family, and school-related confounders is considered, suggesting that interventions targeting well-being may be more immediately informative for this outcome than those targeting achievement alone.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Germany Grade 4 (Reading context; enjoyment of school well-being)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 1 (SRF only): R2=0.331; bullying β=-0.199 (SE=0.020, p<0.001); teacher support β=0.485 (SE=0.023, p<0.001). Model 3 (SRF + post-double selection controls): R2=0.435; bullying β=-0.185 (SE=0.019, p<0.001); teacher support β=0.361 (SE=0.023, p<0.001). Sensitivity (many-worlds): Model 4 R2=0.529 (bullying β=-0.114, p<0.01; teacher support β=0.114, p<0.001); Model 6 R2=0.406 (bullying β=-0.160, p<0.001; teacher support β=0.253, p<0.001); Model 7 R2=0.420 (bullying β=-0.150, p<0.001; teacher support β=0.247, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Germany Grade 4 the study leveraged experienced bullying and perceived teacher support to predict enjoyment of school, finding that both associations remained robustly significant across post-double selection and extensive sensitivity specifications, with bullying consistently negative and teacher support consistently positive. This indicates that strengthening supportive teacher-student relationships and reducing bullying experiences may improve elementary students’ school-related well-being even after accounting for a large set of demographic, cognitive, self-regulated learning, and motivation-related confounders, though the study is observational and cannot establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes representative German PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 data (N=3959) to examine how two social interaction resources—experienced bullying and perceived teacher support—relate to academic track recommendation (a dichotomous proxy for achievement) and enjoyment of school (a standardized well-being measure). Using a double machine learning approach for variable selection (stacked adaptive LASSO across 50 multiple imputations) and OLS with school-clustered robust standard errors, the authors compare baseline and “many-worlds” sensitivity models that expand controls and apply PCA-based dimensionality reduction. For academic track recommendation, the bullying effect shrank from β=-0.062 (Model 1) to β=-0.011 (Model 3) and became non-significant in richer specifications, while teacher support also attenuated. For enjoyment of school, both bullying (e.g., β=-0.185 in Model 3) and teacher support (β=0.361 in Model 3) remained significant across models, with R2 ranging roughly from 0.406 to 0.544. Limitations include observational design, use of track recommendation rather than standardized test scores, and reliance on proxy well-being components (positive affect only).
